intro.text:
A vertical-axis wind turbine: three blades turning in the wind.

How do blades that only go round in circles pull energy out of the air?

captions.text: Wind blows left to right at 8 m/s. The three blades turn anticlockwise at 382 rpm, 2.5 times faster than the wind.
The faint dotted circle is the edge of the rotating part of the mesh. Each blade meets the air at an angle that swings by up to 24° every turn.
On the upwind side the angle grows too large: the blade stalls and sheds a strong vortex. This is dynamic stall.
Most of the power comes just before the stall. A stalled blade briefly brakes the rotor.
Downwind, the blades meet air already slowed by the rotor, and the wakes of the other blades.
The number on top is the power coefficient: the share of the wind's energy the rotor takes. It pulses three times per turn and dips below zero at each stall.

outro.text:
On average the rotor takes 13 % of the wind's energy (Cp = 0.13).
At this speed the blades stall on every turn; spinning faster would keep the angle smaller.
